papers.title: Physical and psychosocial outcomes in children with limb loss 2-years after the 2023 Kahramanmaras-Türkiye earthquakes
papers.abstract: Introduction: The 2023 Kahramanmaras-Turkiye earthquakes resulted in many paediatric amputations. While prosthetic provision following disasters has been described, little is known about longer-term physical and psychosocial outcomes in children with earthquake-related limb loss. Aim: Evaluate health-related quality of life, prosthesis experience, pain, and function approximately two years post-amputation. Method: Retrospective analysis was conducted of children with earthquake-related limb loss who attend the XXX Center. Socio-demographic and amputation-related data, psychological status, outcome scores for pain, the Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) and the Trinity Amputation and Prosthesis Experience Scales (TAPES) were included. Results: Fifty-six children (50% female; 13.7{+/-}5.0 years old) were included. Children had unilateral upper limb loss (n=15), unilateral lower limb loss (n=31), bilateral lower limb loss (n=7), or combined upper and lower limb loss (n=3). Data were obtained 2.3{+/-}0.4 years following amputation. Median child-reported PedsQL scores were 72.3/100.0, with high social functioning (85.0/100.0) but lower emotional functioning (60.0/100.0). No differences in PedsQL outcomes were found between limb loss groups. Children rated their physical and emotional quality of life higher than carers rated them. TAPES median scores were 50.0/75.0 for psychosocial adjustment, 16.0/36.0 for activity restriction, and 34.5/45.0 for prosthetic satisfaction. Children with unilateral lower limb loss demonstrated superior adjustment and prosthetic satisfaction than children with unilateral upper limb or bilateral lower limb loss (p<0.05). Conclusions: Children demonstrated favourable physical, social, and school-related quality of life 2.3 years after the earthquakes. However, emotional wellbeing remained affected, highlighting the importance of long-term mental health support alongside prosthetic and rehabilitation services.

papers.title: Individualized systems-informed corrective exercise for adults meeting prespecified criteria for upper crossed syndrome: protocol for a randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: Background: Heterogeneity in eligibility criteria, intervention content, and exercise-progression rules has limited the reproducibility of research on upper crossed syndrome. This trial will examine the added effect of a structured, individualized, staged corrective-exercise program on adults who meet prespecified criteria for this phenotype. Methods: In this parallel randomized controlled trial, 36 women and men aged 18-40 years with forward head and shoulder posture and increased thoracic kyphosis will be allocated 1:1, stratified by sex. Over 12 weeks, both groups will attend three sessions per week and receive stationary cycling, indication-based stretching and mobilization, and education on healthy movement habits. The intervention group will additionally receive a systems-informed program encompassing restoration of range of motion, muscle-activation retraining, correction of movement patterns, progressive load tolerance, and preparation for health-enhancing physical activity. The primary outcome is the baseline-adjusted week-12 between-group difference in a multivariate profile comprising the forward-head, forward-shoulder, and thoracic-kyphosis angles. Scapular-muscle electromyography, range of motion, and balance are secondary outcomes. The primary exploratory electroencephalographic outcome is change in central relative alpha power during quiet standing with eyes open. Posture, range of motion, and balance will be assessed at baseline, week 12, and four-week follow-up; electromyography and electroencephalography at baseline and week 12. The primary analysis will use MANCOVA adjusted for baseline and sex, with Pillai's trace; longitudinal analyses will use linear mixed models. Effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals will be reported. Conclusions: This study will test the added effect of a reproducible corrective-exercise framework beyond the shared active-control components. The four-week follow-up will not support inference about long-term prevention of recurrence. Ethics and trial registration: Ethics approval: IR.UI.REC.1404.053. Trial registration: IRCT20250921067305N1.

papers.title: User Experience of a Rehab Community-Based, Affordable Robot Exercise System (Rehab CARES) for Gamified Motor and Cognitive Stroke Rehabilitation
papers.abstract: Purpose: Robot-assisted therapy predominantly targets motor impairment, although post-stroke motor and cognitive impairments co-occur. We report user experience in a longitudinal deployment of a Rehab Community-based Affordable Robot Exercise System (RehabCARES) for delivering personalized motor/cognitive training. Methods: Six adults with chronic stroke (FM-UE 20-61; MoCA 22-28) completed 12 therapy visits with THEAbot, a reconfigurable 1-DoF robot. Rehab CARES also included a haptic/biometric dynamic difficulty adjustment controller and eight games characterized by cognitive processes and motor/cognitive demand. We report gaming preference, usage, and user experience (pain, exertion, usability, affect, workload) across therapy. Results: User experience varied, but generally, self-reported pain was low, perceived exertion was light to moderate, enjoyment was strong and stable, and sense of control increased while excitement plateaued. Workload showed decreasing frustration and effort. Game selection during therapy was partially consistent with motor/cognitive clinical profiles; preferences and perceptual abilities may have influenced choices. Usability scores exceeded acceptability at all time points, peaking at the final visit (86 +/- 4.5 out of 100). Conclusions: RehabCARES provided personalized motor/cognitive training to a heterogeneous cohort in a community-based setting, delivering a positive user experience. Hardware reconfigurability and motor/cognitive game variety likely enabled this success.

papers.title: Early Prediction of Discharge Outcomes in Geriatric Rehabilitation: Development and Temporal Validation of a Multiclass Model
papers.abstract: To develop and validate a model that predicts on day 7 of subacute rehabilitation (timed to inform the first multidisciplinary team meeting) the probabilities of three mutually exclusive outcomes: minimal dependency, nursing-care dependency, or medical deterioration. Design: Retrospective cohort study with temporal validation. Multinomial regression and XGBoost models were trained on 80% of admissions during the years 2016-2024 of members of the largest national health maintenance organization (HMO), tested on the remaining 20% and members of other HMOs, and validated on year 2025 admissions. Models output patient-level outcome probabilities with the strongest feature contributors. Setting: A public geriatric rehabilitation hospital. Participants: All consecutive first admissions (N=10,920; median age 80 years; median length of stay 35 days). Interventions: Not applicable. Main Outcome Measures: Discharge disposition: minimal dependency, nursing-care dependency, or medical deterioration (transfer to acute care without return, or in-hospital death). Predictors were demographic, functional, cognitive, clinical, and laboratory variables documented before day 7 with linkage to pre-admission community health records. Performance was assessed by multiclass area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Brier score and positive predictive value (PPV). Results: Overall, 34% of patients were discharged with minimal dependency, 44% with nursing-care dependency, and 22% deteriorated medically. Both models performed comparably. Multinomial regression achieved an AUC of 0.81 (95% CI: 0.79-0.83) compared with 0.72 (0.71-0.73) for FIM alone, and it was maintained on temporal validation (AUC 0.80, 0.78-0.82). At a [≥]60% probability threshold, the model flagged 32% of patients for nursing-care dependency and 5% for deterioration, with PPVs of 72% and 69%, respectively. Conclusions: Day-7 multiclass risk estimation from routinely collected data is feasible, interpretable and stable over time. Alerts could prompt earlier social-work involvement and closer monitoring of patients at risk of deterioration; prospective controlled evaluation is warranted.

papers.title: Five Days of Acute Intermittent Hypoxia Is Safe and Improves Somatic Motor Function in Persons with Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES Walking impairment affects up to 75% of persons with multiple sclerosis (MS), and the benefits of rehabilitation are constrained by limited capacity for training-induced neuroplasticity. Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH), brief repeated exposures to low inspired oxygen, triggers serotonin-dependent spinal plasticity that enhances motor output. In spinal cord injury, daily AIH paired with walking training has produced larger walking gains than training alone, positioning AIH as a promising primer for rehabilitation. Before AIH can be combined with training in MS, its safety and stand-alone effects with repeated daily dosing must be established in a population with demyelinating disease. We therefore conducted the first multi-day AIH trial in persons with MS to characterize safety and tolerability and to evaluate preliminary effects on ankle strength and walking. METHODS Twenty-three ambulatory adults with MS (Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] 3.0-6.5; 15 relapsing-remitting, 8 secondary-progressive) completed a randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Participants received AIH (15 x ~60 s episodes; FiO2 = 0.09; SpO2 target 84-88%) and Sham in a counterbalanced order, separated by a washout of at least 4 weeks. Assessments at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and follow-up included ankle plantarflexion and dorsiflexion torque, 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT), Timed 25-Foot Walk (T25FW), and MS Walking Scale-12 (MSWS-12). Treatment effects were estimated using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) with participant as a random effect. RESULTS No serious adverse events related to the intervention were reported, and follow-up MRI showed no new MS activity in either arm. Mean nadir SpO2 during AIH was 84.7 +/- 0.2%, and cardiovascular parameters returned to baseline within minutes of each session completion. Ankle plantarflexion torque was significantly greater following AIH than Sham (beta = 8.74 Nm, p < 0.001), with mean increases of 17.5% at post-intervention and 29.2% at follow-up. Six-minute walk distance was also significantly greater after AIH (beta = 10.14 m, p = 0.039). Dorsiflexion torque (p = 0.202), T25FW time (p = 0.239), and MSWS-12 score (p = 0.564) did not differ significantly between conditions. Greater elevation in heart rate during hypoxic episodes was associated with larger strength gains at follow-up (r = 0.58, p = 0.009). CONCLUSIONS: Daily AIH sessions are safe and well tolerated in persons with MS across a clinically heterogeneous disability range and produce significant improvements in ankle plantarflexion strength and walking endurance. These findings support combining AIH with task-specific gait training in future trials.

papers.title: Regression-Based Balance Discordance Refines Prediction of Prospective Falls After Subacute Stroke: A Secondary Analysis of the LEAPS Trial
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo determine whether continuous, regression-based measures of balance discordance refine prediction of prospective, recurrent falls after subacute stroke relative to a previously published threshold-based classification in the same cohort, and to characterize how a purely data-driven, dimensionality-reduction-based composite expresses the same underlying measures. DesignSecondary, observational analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Recurrent falls were modeled using Andersen-Gill Cox proportional hazards regression with robust standard errors clustered by participant. SettingFive-site, National Institutes of Health/National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke funded multicenter trial (Locomotor Experience Applied Post-Stroke, LEAPS). Participants384 adults with subacute stroke (of 408 randomized in the parent trial) with valid baseline balance confidence, walking, and balance scores and at least one recorded follow-up interval (2,357 person-intervals, 179 fall events). Main Outcome MeasuresProspective, recurrent falls over 12 months, ascertained via self-report falls diary. Balance discordance was computed as the residual from regressing balance confidence on objective walking distance, Berg Balance Scale performance, or both jointly (multivariable discordance); threshold-based classification used established cut-points on the same measures and principal component analysis served as secondary comparators. ResultsSingle-variable discordance was associated with lower fall hazard (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.79, 95% CI 0.63-0.99, p = .037), and multivariable discordance was associated with higher fall hazard (HR = 1.27, 95% CI 1.03-1.58, p = .026). None of three threshold-based classification indicators reached significance. Multivariable discordance and a three-component principal-component composite showed comparable model fit (concordance 0.616 vs. 0.618) and were substantially correlated (R2 = .49). ConclusionsContinuous, regression-based balance discordance predicted prospective, recurrent falls where a previously published threshold-based classification did not. The divergent direction of single- and multivariable findings suggests overconfidence relative to combined objective function, rather than confidence broadly, may be the more specific marker of fall risk.

papers.title: The development and psychometric evaluation of the Post Activity Symptom Scale (PASS) for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/ Chronic Fatigue Syndrome.
papers.abstract: PurposeTo develop and psychometrically evaluate a new scale measuring post-exertional malaise in people with myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME)/ chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS). MethodsA draft scale was co-produced with patient and clinician advisory groups. After extensive pilot testing, adults with ME/CFS completed the Post Activity Symptom Scale online and repeated it two weeks later to assess test-retest reliability and sensitivity to change. Rasch analysis assessed each domain for unidimensionality, targeting, internal reliability, item fit and local dependency. Then Rasch-transformed interval data and parametric statistics were used to assess criterion-related and discriminant validity (by comparison with measures of physical health and ME/CFS severity), test-retest reliability and minimal detectable difference. ResultsThe item regarding delay in PEM onset was an under-discriminating misfit anomaly which was inconsistent with the remaining PASS items. When this was removed, the PASS was a unidimensional, psychometrically robust scale. Criterion-related validity (r=0.58, p<0.001) was moderate and highly significant, discriminant validity (p<0.001) and test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.81) were excellent. The minimal detectable difference was 1.93/100. Participants found the PASS easy to complete, comprehensive and relevant. ConclusionThe Post Activity Symptom Scale is a valid, reliable, sensitive measure of people of PEM in ME/CFS

papers.title: Midlife mobility assessment from the pocket: agreement and consistency between smartphone placement configurations
papers.abstract: Subtle declines in mobility may emerge during midlife and can be detected using smartphone-based motion measures. Instrumented assessment of balance and functional tasks commonly uses lower-back placement, which requires device fixation and may limit convenient real-world monitoring. This study compared mobility outcomes obtained from a practical front-pocket/thigh placement with those from a standardized lower-back placement during static balance, sit-to-stand (STS), and Timed Up and Go (TUG) tests. Forty-six adults aged 40-64 years completed static balance, 30-second STS, and TUG assessments during simultaneous smartphone recording at the lower back and pocket/thigh. Outcomes included two- and three-dimensional sway, STS repetition count, average repetition duration, lower limb power, and maximal vertical velocity, as well as TUG total duration and peak yaw angular velocity during both turns. Associations, intraclass correlation coefficients, and Bland-Altman analyses were used to characterize the relationship and agreement between the two placements. Balance outcomes showed strong correlations between placements (rs=0.83-0.93), with moderate-to-excellent consistency for most conditions, although pocket/thigh sway values were systematically higher. TUG total duration showed strong correlation and good absolute agreement (rs=0.895; ICC=0.881), and turning velocity showed good consistency during the first and the second turns. STS repetition count and average repetition duration demonstrated strong correlations between placements (r=0.996 and 0.985, respectively), with excellent absolute agreement for repetition count and excellent consistency for average repetition duration (ICC=0.993 and 0.982, respectively). In contrast, STS power and maximal vertical velocity showed weaker correlations and consistency (r=0.709 and rs=0.382; ICC=0.600 and 0.417, respectively). Pocket/thigh smartphone placement supports practical mobility assessment across balance, STS and TUG. Although some movement-derived measures showed placement-dependent differences in absolute values, relative performance patterns were generally preserved across placements. These findings support the development of pocket-based smartphone assessment for simplified and potentially unsupervised mobility monitoring in midlife, while placement-sensitive outcomes require further validation against external reference measures. Author SummaryWearable technologies, including smartphones, offer promising ways to assess mobility during midlife, when subtle changes in physical performance may begin to emerge but go undetected by conventional clinical tests. However, most research using these technologies has been conducted under controlled conditions, with devices often attached to the lower back. Although this approach provides useful measurements, it requires fixation, making it less practical for everyday use. In this study, we examined whether smartphones carried in a front pocket could provide mobility measurements comparable to those obtained from the lower back. Forty-six middle-aged adults completed balance, chair-standing, and walking and turning tasks while smartphones recorded their movements at both locations. We found that measures of mobility, such as chair-standing repetitions and walking task completion time, were highly comparable between smartphone locations. Balance measurements, such as body sway while standing on one leg, showed similar patterns, although their absolute values differed. In contrast, measures of muscle power and maximum upward movement speed during chair-standing were more sensitive to smartphone placement. Our findings support the potential of pocket-based smartphone assessment as a practical approach to measuring mobility beginning in midlife, while further research is needed to establish its suitability for everyday use.

papers.title: Development and psychometric evaluation of the Severity of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Scale (SoMES) and the Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS)
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and psychometrically evaluate two new brief assessments measuring disease severity (the Severity of ME Scale, SoMES) and occupational status (the ME Occupational Status Scale, MEOSS) in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) MethodsDraft SoMES and MEOSS were co-produced from relevant literature and lived experience. An online survey completed by adults with ME/CFS and was repeated two weeks later to assess reliability. The SF-36 (physical function) assessed criterion-related validity (Spearmann correlations) and discriminant validity (Kruskal-Wallis tests). Weighted kappa co-efficients assessed test-retest reliability and measurement error calculated minimal detectable difference (MDD). Results995 adults with ME/CFS participated and 579 completed the retest survey. Construct validity was confirmed from feedback. Criterion related validity was moderate-good (SoMES r = 0.663, MEOSS r=0.472, both p<0.001). Discriminant validity was demonstrated by significant differences in SF36-PF scores in different levels of SoMES and MEOSS (p=0.003 - 0.0001). SoMES test-retest reliability was moderate (k =0.53, P<0.001) with a MDD of 1.6, and excellent for the MEOSS (k = 0.76 p<.001) and the MDD was 1.4 ConclusionsThe Severity of ME Scale (SoMES) and the ME Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS) are valid, reliable, sensitive assessments of ME/CFS severity and occupational status respectively.

papers.title: LOW-FREQUENCY DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION PROMOTES LONG-TERM OROFACIAL MOTOR RECOVERY AFTER TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY: A CASE STUDY
papers.abstract: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI), a subtype of traumatic brain injury (TBI), can disrupt corticobulbar pathways, leading to chronic deficits in speech and swallowing. We present a first-in-human case study demonstrating the long-term therapeutic potential of low-frequency continuous deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the motor thalamus to restore corticobulbar function in a patient with severe DAI and persistent dysarthria and dysphagia. The patient underwent bilateral motor thalamus DBS implantation one-year post-injury for treatment of post-traumatic action tremor, and stimulation was delivered chronically at 55 Hz over three years of follow-up. We assessed orofacial motor outcomes using kinematic analysis of facial movements, videofluoroscopic swallowing studies, and speech tasks to dissociate the immediate assistive effects of stimulation (DBS ON versus OFF) from its long-term therapeutic effects (DBS OFF over time). Continuous DBS led to progressive recovery of facial symmetry, resolution of laryngeal penetration, and marked improvements in respiratory and phonatory control and speech intelligibility. While improvements in gross orofacial motor function persisted in the absence of stimulation, fine articulatory control remained dependent on ongoing stimulation or adjunct speech therapy for optimal performance. Stimulation-induced improvements in cervical posture may also have contributed to enhanced biomechanics of swallowing and voice production. These findings provide early evidence that low-frequency motor thalamus DBS may promote therapeutic benefits and extend the window of functional recovery in chronic TBI patients.

papers.title: Smaller Cortical Responses to Balance Perturbations in Parkinson's Disease with Freezing of Gait
papers.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) is among the most disabling symptoms of Parkinsons disease (PD) and is associated with balance impairment and increased falls risk, yet remains challenging to understand due to its episodic and context-dependent nature. Altered supplementary motor area (SMA) function at rest and before self-initiated movements has been implicated in FoG; however, whether this extends to functionally relevant balance behavior is unknown. A loss of balance in response to support surface translations during standing elicits a perturbation-evoked N1 potential, an error assessment signal linked to SMA activity. We therefore predicted that people with FoG would have smaller and later N1 responses than people with PD without FoG and older adults. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) during backward support-surface translations in 29 people with PD (71 {+/-} 7 years), including 13 people with a history of FoG (FoG+) and 16 people without FoG (FoG-), and 26 older adults (OA; 67 {+/-} 6 years). N1 amplitude and latency were quantified at a central midline electrode and defined as the largest negative peak 100-300 ms post-perturbation. N1 responses were similar between OA and FoG-({Delta} = 4.0 {micro}V and 2.8 ms, respectively). In contrast, FoG+ had smaller N1 amplitudes than FoG- ({Delta} = 18.1 {micro}V, p = 0.001) and OA ({Delta} = 14.1 {micro}V, p = 0.003), and both differences persisted after adjusting for age. FoG+ also had later N1 latencies than OA ({Delta} = 26.5 ms, p = 0.029), with a similar but non-significant difference versus FoG- ({Delta} = 23.6 ms, p = 0.091); after adjusting for age, these latency differences were not retained. These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked cortical activity is altered in FoG, potentially reflecting altered SMA function, and may provide a functionally relevant marker of FoG susceptibility.

papers.title: Effects of Weighted Seated Core Exercises on Immediate Postural Stability in Healthy Young Adults: An Exploratory Study
papers.abstract: ObjectivesThis exploratory study investigated whether low-load, seated core exercises could produce immediate improvements in standing balance among healthy young adults, aiming to provide a foundation for safe, early-stage rehabilitation protocols. MethodsTen healthy males performed seated core exercises consisted of alternating hip flexion 5 times per side while seated and maintaining bilateral shoulder flexion at 120{degrees} shoulder flexion under four load conditions: upper-limb weight only, a 400-g empty box, a 1-kg ball, and a 2-kg ball. Immediately following the exercise, participants performed a 10-s single-leg stance. Transversus abdominis (TrA) thickness was measured via wireless ultrasound at baseline, post-exercise, and during the stance. Center of pressure (CoP) sway was recorded concurrently to evaluate postural stability. ResultsLeft-side TrA thickness during stance increased significantly under the 1-kg and 2-kg load conditions compared to baseline (p 0.05). A moderate positive correlation ({rho} = 0.43, p = 0.002) was found between right-side TrA thickness and CoP sway velocity during the single-leg stance. ConclusionsLow-load, seated core exercises do not yield immediate enhancements in standing stability in healthy populations. The results suggest that increased TrA thickness during a balance task may correlate with heightened postural instability rather than improved balance control. Further research is needed to determine whether these findings translate to clinical populations with impaired physical fitness.

papers.title: Technology Demonstration of a Portable Sensorimotor Assessment System after Short-Duration Spaceflight
papers.abstract: Astronauts experience sensorimotor dysfunction due to microgravity-induced adaptations, leading to impaired posture, locomotion, and manual control. This manuscript details a portable sensorimotor assessment system, including an ankle proprioception test and visual-vestibular tests in a virtual reality headset, which was successfully deployed as a technology demonstration for one astronaut participant pre- and post-spaceflight. Post-flight testing occurred 1 and 3 days after return to Earth (R+1, R+3), with ankle proprioception also tested at R+0. Compared to pre-flight, left ankle proprioception was decreased at R+0 (two standard deviations below the mean of normative data) and returned to pre-flight levels by R+1. All visual-vestibular parameters showed decreased performance post-flight (below the 25th percentile of normative data) and little recovery by R+3. While future validation is required, these assessments appear sensitive to post-flight sensorimotor deconditioning. Furthermore, this technology demonstration highlights the logistical considerations and operational compatibility of the assessments post-flight.

papers.title: Therapeutic acute intermittent hypoxia alters supraspinal neural control of lower limb movement in multiple sclerosis
papers.abstract: Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) therapy is a promising neurorehabilitative intervention with well- documented improvement in motor function in people with spinal cord injury. Its effect on lower-limb motor control in multiple sclerosis (MS), where walking impairment is a leading source of disability, remain uncharacterized, and the supraspinal effects of AIH therapy are unknown. In a sham-controlled, double-blind crossover trial (NCT05164705), 23 adults with MS completed 5 sessions of AIH therapy and of sham therapy; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed before and after each therapeutic intervention. At each timepoint, blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) functional MRI was collected during a repeated plantar- and dorsi-flexion task. Task-evoked activation was modeled at the group level and compared across timepoint and therapeutic arm. Activation changes differed for the left- and right-foot task. AIH augmented activation in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and cortical motor regions during left-foot movement with similar but sub-threshold patterns for the right foot. Right-foot movement additionally showed enhanced deactivation in prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, although these effects were primarily in white matter voxels, limiting their interpretability. These findings suggest that changes in subcortical activation may contribute to motor function improvements following AIH therapy, implicating the basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical motor loop as a target of AIH-induced neuroplasticity. These results also indicate that AIH therapy modulates supraspinal motor circuitry, supporting further investigation of the cortical and subcortical effects of this emerging therapeutic treatment.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Plyometric Exercises Versus Flatfoot Corrective Exercises on Balance and Foot Posture in Obese Children with a Flexible Flatfoot: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: Background and PurposeChildhood obesity often leads to flexible flatfoot, which negatively affects foot posture, balance, and physical function. While exercise is commonly used in clinical practice, there is limited comparative evidence on plyometric training versus traditional corrective exercises in this population. This study aimed to compare the effects of an 8-week plyometric exercise program versus flatfoot corrective exercises on balance and foot posture in obese children aged 7-11 years with flexible flatfoot. MethodsA parallel, non-randomized comparative study was conducted with 120 children recruited from schools in Bengaluru. Participants were allocated to either Group A (plyometric exercises, n = 60) or Group B (flatfoot corrective exercises, n = 60). Both groups trained for 8 weeks (two 40-minute sessions weekly). Foot posture was assessed using the Foot Posture Index-6 (FPI-6), and static balance was measured as center-of-pressure path length using the BTrackS Balance Tracking System before and after the intervention. ResultsBoth groups demonstrated statistically significant within-group improvements in foot posture and balance after 8 weeks (p < 0.001). However, the plyometric group achieved slightly better improvements in foot posture (statistically significant for the left foot, p = 0.028) and markedly greater gains in balance (median path length: 30.39 cm vs. 37.45 cm, p< 0.001) compared to the corrective exercise group. ConclusionsBoth exercise approaches are beneficial for obese children with flexible flatfoot. Plyometric training provides additional advantages in improving dynamic balance and neuromuscular control, supporting its inclusion in pediatric physiotherapy programs.

papers.title: A Retrospective Real-World Assessment of Motor Status After Stroke Using a Home-Based Brain-Computer Interface
papers.abstract: BackgroundUpper extremity impairment persists in many stroke survivors, and few treatments are effective for severe chronic deficits. Brain-computer interface (BCI) therapy, which pairs decoded motor-intention-associated electrophysiology with sensory feedback, has improved upper extremity impairment in randomized trials, including in patients with severe paresis. Whether these benefits translate to routine care has rarely been evaluated. This study examined upper extremity motor recovery through 1 year among patients prescribed at-home BCI therapy in clinical practice. MethodsThis retrospective observational study included adults who were prescribed the IpsiHand System, an electroencephalography-based BCI, through a commercial US home therapy program, had a baseline Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) assessment, and averaged >1 session per week through their last assessment. Occupational therapists administered the UEFM by video every 4 weeks. The primary outcome was UEFM change from baseline to week 12. A mixed model for repeated measures estimated change through week 52, with multiple imputation sensitivity analyses for missing data. ResultsOf 452 patients included in analyses (mean time since stroke, 5.4{+/-}5.4 years), mean baseline UEFM was 20.1{+/-}14.6, with 333 patients (73.7%) having severe motor impairment (UEFM 0-28). At week 12, mean UEFM change was 4.3 points (95% CI, 3.7-4.9; P<0.001), and 31.7% achieved the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 5.25 points. Mean change reached the MCID at week 16 (5.6, 95% CI [4.8, 6.4]). Model-estimated change in UEFM continued to improve through 1 year, being 6.1 (95% CI, 5.5-6.8) at week 24 and 8.1 (95% CI, 6.8-9.4) at week 52. ConclusionsAmong regular users of at-home BCI therapy in routine care, most of whom had severe chronic impairment, UEFM scores improved by 12 weeks, reached MCID by 16 weeks, and continued to increase through 1 year. At-home BCI therapy merits evaluation in randomized trials with follow-up beyond 12 weeks.

papers.title: Predicting Robot-Based Tracking Performance After Stroke Using Lesion Features and Clinical Assessments: A Pilot Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundFollowing stroke, motor and cognitive impairments often limit functional independence. Personalized rehabilitation requires comprehensive clinical assessments, which are costly and time-consuming. Imaging scans are routinely collected, but their predictive value in determining post-stroke function remains unclear. ObjectivesTo determine the ability of clinical assessments, lesion features with medical chart information, and a combined clinical and biomedical model to predict kinematic outcomes from a robot-based tracking task in chronic stroke individuals. MethodsEighteen participants (70{+/-}6 years) completed a robot-based tracking task and a battery of motor and cognitive assessments. Three elastic net regression models were developed: 1) clinical assessments only; 2) lesion metrics and chart information only; and 3) a combined model. Models were evaluated using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, bootstrapping, and permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Robot-based outcomes included tracking error, normalized distance, velocity error response, and delay. ResultsThe clinical assessment model significantly predicted tracking error (R{superscript 2}=0.45), delay (R{superscript 2}=0.22), velocity error response (R{superscript 2}=0.18), and normalized distance (R{superscript 2}=0.12). The combined model significantly predicted tracking error (R{superscript 2}=0.37), delay (R{superscript 2}=0.19), and velocity error response (R{superscript 2}=0.11). The imaging model did not significantly predict any outcome. Box and Blocks Test and Color Trails 1 were stable features. The right dorsal attention network was a stable predictor in several combined models. ConclusionClinical assessments outperformed lesion features in predicting tracking performance after chronic stroke. Attention- and motor-related measures were the strongest predictors, highlighting the importance of cognitive-motor interactions in function. A larger sample and more granular lesion features may improve prediction from imaging biomarkers.

papers.title: Remote Ischemic Conditioning Modulates Spinal Reflex Excitability in Healthy Young Adults: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundRemote ischemic conditioning (RIC), involving transient and sublethal bouts of ischemia and reperfusion, promotes neuroplasticity and motor learning. Although early clinical studies suggest supraspinal and muscular mechanisms underlying RIC, its influence on spinal reflex excitability - a key substrate for motor learning - remains poorly understood. Balance training alone is known to modulate spinal excitability, but whether RIC can enhance this training-induced adaptation has not been tested. ObjectiveThis prospective single-blind, pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) explored the preliminary effects of pairing RIC with balance training on spinal reflex excitability and balance performance in healthy young adults and generated estimates of variability to inform a future definitive randomized trial. MethodsTwenty-six participants aged between 18-40 years were randomized to RIC or sham groups at university-based research setting between March and August 2025. The intervention included five cycles of 5-minute cuff inflation (RIC: 200 mmHg; sham: 25 mmHg) and 5-minute deflation on the dominant thigh, followed by balance training on a stability platform (15 trials/day) for five consecutive days. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included Hoffmanns reflex (H-reflex) parameters--Hmax (peak H-reflex amplitude reflecting motor neuron recruitment via Ia afferent input), H/M ratio (Hmax normalized to maximal M-wave amplitude), Hslp/Mslp ratio (relative slope of the H-reflex and M-wave recruitment curves), and H-reflex threshold (minimum stimulus intensity eliciting a response)--used to index spinal motor neuron pool excitability, as well as balance performance, quantified as center time (the duration participants maintained a stability platform within a set horizontal threshold). Independent sample and Mann-Whitney U tests analyzed the differences in the change scores (RIC vs Sham) for H-reflex and balance outcomes respectively. ResultsThe RIC group showed directionally greater reduction in the Hslp/ Mslp ratio (p = 0.02) and greater improvement in balance performance (p = 0.02) compared to sham group. No significant between-group differences were observed for Hmax, H/M ratio, or H-reflex threshold; however, the direction of changes in Hmax was consistent with reduced spinal reflex excitability following RIC. These findings potentially suggest that RIC could augment the neuroplastic adaptations typically induced by balance training. ConclusionThis pilot study provides preliminary evidence that RIC paired with balance training may influence selected spinal neurophysiological responses and improve balance performance in healthy adults. The potential convergence of neurophysiological and behavioral adaptations observed in this pilot study may suggest a role for RIC as a physiological primer for sensorimotor learning. Moreover, these findings establish a foundation for future large-scale trials incorporating cortical and presynaptic inhibitory measures to elucidate mechanisms and clinical applicability in neurological populations.

papers.title: Evaluating ChatGPTs Responses to Chiropractic Patient Questions: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are used at an increased frequency by patients to answer health related questions. Prior studies have evaluated LLMs and their performance with musculoskeletal (MSK) and spine domains, but have not been used to evaluate chiropractic-relevant content. ObjectiveTo evaluate ChatGPT responses to commonly asked chiropractic patient questions for concordance with chiropractic clinical practice guidelines. MethodsThirty questions addressing low back pain, neck pain, and chronic musculoskeletal pain were developed based on current U.S. chiropractic clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). ChatGPT (GPT-5.2) generated responses in isolated sessions. Responses were assessed for readability using established indices, then five licensed chiropractors independently rated each response using a 5-point Likert scale across four domains: relevance, clarity, completeness, and accuracy. Inter-rater reliability was evaluated using Krippendorffs alpha (ordinal). ResultsReadability measures demonstrated that ChatGPT responses were written at approximately a college-level reading grade. Expert ratings across all domain means (standard deviation) were predominately clustered at the upper end of rating scale (1-5): Relevance 4.72 {+/-} 0.56; Clarity 4.76 {+/-} 0.50; Completeness 4.23 {+/-} 0.81; Accuracy 4.00 {+/-} 1.02. The Krippendorffs alpha (ordinal) ranged from -0.023-0.214 across the domains, all reflective of poor inter-rater reliability. ConclusionChatGPT responses were broadly consistent with chiropractic CPGs, though readability levels exceeded recommended patient education standards. While the expert panel frequently assigned similar scores, minor scoring differences and restricted score distributions produced low chance-corrected reliability. These findings suggest that ChatGPT can produce guideline concordant responses but readability and interpretive variability should be considered when integrating LLM generated information into patient education.

papers.title: Acceptability, Safety and Feasibility of a Sedentary Behaviour Intervention (REACH-SCI) in Individuals with Spinal Cord Injury: A Mixed-Methods Study
papers.abstract: PurposeIndividuals with paraplegia often have high levels of sedentary behaviour, which increases cardiovascular disease risk. This study assessed the acceptability, safety and feasibility of a sedentary behaviour intervention (REACH-SCI) in individuals with paraplegia. Materials and methodsA pre-post feasibility study was conducted in wheelchair-users with paraplegia (n=18) to evaluate an 8-week intervention comprised of a wearable activity tracker, educational booklet, goal setting, motivational support sessions, peer support and activity tools (Trial registration: NCT06957483). Acceptability was assessed via semi-structured interviews and questionnaires, safety via adverse events, pain and fatigue, and intervention feasibility via components being delivered as intended. Intervention engagement and preliminary efficacy were also assessed. ResultsThe intervention and study procedures were acceptable and safe, intervention components were delivered as planned, and the study was feasible in terms of participant recruitment, retention and data completion rates. Engagement with intervention components was generally high, except for peer support. The intervention demonstrated preliminary efficacy for improving sedentary behaviour, physical activity, cardiovascular disease biomarkers and psychosocial outcomes. ConclusionsAn intervention to reduce sedentary behaviour in individuals with paraplegia was acceptable, safe and feasible. The effectiveness of REACH-SCI should be evaluated in a definitive trial to inform clinical care and public health guidelines.

papers.title: Single-Case Design for Network-based BCI Rehabilitation: Individual Learning Trajectories and Effects of Motor Imagery Timing in Stroke Patients
papers.abstract: BackgroundMotor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are increasingly investigated for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, it remains unclear how BCI control improves through repeated training in stroke patients and whether the timing of MI decoding systematically influences this trajectory. MethodsTo address this question, we implemented a single-case experimental design involving five chronic stroke patients enrolling in a longitudinal electroencephalography MI-BCI training involving their affected hand. Across 18 sessions conducted over six weeks, the onset of a fixed-duration MI decoding window was randomized to occur 1, 2, or 3 s after cue onset according to an alternating-treatments single-case design. Notably, the BCI combined spectral power and functional connectivity features to classify MI states. ResultsThe MI classification timing had no significant effect on BCI accuracy, fatigue, or spasticity. BCI accuracy increased across training in four of five patients and was accompanied by patient-specific longitudinal changes in local spectral activity and functional connectivity. These convergent trajectories were consistent with acquisition of BCI control, but were not accompanied by clinically meaningful improvement in motor function. ConclusionsVarying the onset of the MI decoding window provided no systematic benefit for BCI control. Instead, differences in neurophysiological trajectories across patients indicate that MI decoding parameters need to be personalized and reassessed throughout the training. Overall, these findings inform more individualized and effective BCI settings for neuromotor stroke rehabilitation. Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06951035, registered 30 April 2025

papers.title: Effectiveness of Kalevala Manual Therapy, Health Coaching, and Physiotherapy for Chronic Low Back Pain: A Randomized Controlled Trial (The INTEGRA Trial)
papers.abstract: Background and aimLow back pain is the leading cause of years lived with disability (YLDs) globally. While physiotherapy (PT) is recommended as a first-line treatment, evidence regarding Kalevala Manual Therapy (KMT) remains limited. This study compared the effects of physiotherapy, KMT, and KMT combined with health coaching (KMT+HC) on pain, disability, and psychosocial outcomes in individuals with CLBP. Experimental procedureIn this single-center, three-arm, parallel-group trial, 81 adults with non-specific CLBP (symptoms [≥] 12 weeks, STarT Back score > 3) were randomized (1:1:1) to receive PT (n = 27), KMT (n = 27), or KMT+HC (n = 27) over an 8-week intervention period. Primary outcomes were functional disability (Oswestry Disability Index, ODI) and pain intensity (Numeric Rating Scale, NRS). Secondary outcomes included work- and physical activity-related fear-avoidance beliefs (FABQ-W, FABQ-PA), depressive symptoms (BDI), quality of life (RAND-36), and patient-specific functional status (PSFS). Longitudinal changes were analyzed using linear mixed models. ResultsStatistically significant and generally clinically meaningful improvements over time were observed across the intervention groups for both ODI and NRS (both p < 0.001), with no significant between-group differences in the primary outcomes. No significant between-group differences were identified for the primary outcomes. A significant group-by-time interaction was observed for work-related fear-avoidance beliefs (FABQ-W; p = 0.005). Post hoc analyses revealed that KMT+HC achieved a significantly greater reduction in FABQ-W scores than PT (p = 0.002), with only the KMT+HC group exceeding the established minimal clinically important difference (MCID) threshold. Overall treatment satisfaction was high, with a mean score of at least 6.2 out of 7 and 100% protocol adherence were observed across all arms without any reported adverse events. ConclusionKMT and KMT combined with health coaching produced improvements in pain and functional disability comparable to guideline-based physiotherapy. Furthermore, the addition of structured health coaching to KMT significantly reduced work-related fear-avoidance beliefs, demonstrating the value of integrating behavioral support into manual therapy for comprehensive CLBP rehabilitation.

papers.title: Upright Participation for Learners with Physical Disabilities: A Pilot Randomized Crossover Effectiveness-Implementation Trial of Robot-assisted Walking in Schools
papers.abstract: BackgroundSchool-based implementation of robot-assisted walking may support increased physical and social participation for children with physical disabilities, but evidence from an adequately powered trial is needed. This pilot study evaluated implementation strategies and study procedures to inform a future definitive trial. MethodsParticipants were randomized to 12-weeks of robot-assisted walking or control, with subsequent crossover to the other condition. In the intervention arm, targeted dose was 75 minutes of robot-assisted walking, spread across three days/week. Implementation strategies for the childs classroom team included educational materials, centralized technical assistance, school champions, and on-going training. Implementation strategy evaluation focused on intervention protocol feasibility (i.e., weekly device use, troubleshooting) and fidelity (documentation of implementation strategy modifications). Preliminary estimates participation goal changes were obtained using the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) Performance scale (/10). ResultsEight children with neurodevelopmental physical disabilities participated (mean age 3.5, SD 0.5 years). Device use varied from 2.1 to 4.3 days/week (median 3.3) with a range of 48 to 96 minutes/week (median 80). Target use of [≥] 3 days/week was achieved for 66% of weeks and met the [≥]75-minute target for 33% of weeks. Troubleshooting occurred in 18.5% of sessions. Two implementation strategies were modified to improve feasibility. COPM mean change was 3.56 (SD 1.07) for robot-assisted walking and 2.11 (SD 2.41) for control (dz=0.74). ConclusionsThis pilot study provided preliminary evidence regarding both the feasibility of robot-assisted walking implementation in schools and its potential effectiveness for children with physical disabilities. Findings support progression to a definitive trial.

papers.title: Feasibility of Distributed Wearable Ultrasound for Detecting Neuromuscular Coordination Differences After Knee Injury
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThe aim of the current study was to evaluate the feasibility of a multi-channel distributed wearable ultrasound (D-WUS) system capable of simultaneously probing dynamic muscle activity across multiple anatomical sites to assess neuromuscular coordination during physical activity. MethodsTwenty NCAA Division I women athletes (8 with prior knee injury) performed countermovement jumps (CMJs) on dual force plates while wearing a four-channel D-WUS system targeting the vastus lateralis (VL) and vastus medialis oblique (VMO) in both limbs. Real-time M-mode ultrasound data were processed using a composite factorization approach integrating nonnegative matrix factorization and principal component analysis (CF-PCA) to extract dominant muscle-contraction patterns. Correlation and timing metrics between VL and VMO were compared across injury status. ResultsCMJ performance metrics (jump height, RSImod) did not differ between groups (p > 0.05). However, D-WUS revealed significant differences in muscle coordination in the right limb: VL-VMO correlation (p = 0.029) and timing symmetry (p = 0.019) were reduced in participants with prior knee injury; left-limb differences were not significant. Right-limb timing symmetry was negatively correlated with SMFA score ({rho} = -0.48, p = 0.033). Functional survey scores (SMFA) also differed significantly (p = 0.001), while VISA-P scores did not. ConclusionThese preliminary findings provide feasibility-level evidence that distributed wearable ultrasound can detect limb-specific neuromuscular coordination differences not reflected in force-plate biomechanics, motivating larger prospective studies to establish reliability and clinical utility. SignificanceWith further validation, this approach may offer a scalable, objective means of monitoring muscle contraction during rehabilitation.

papers.title: Development of a Communication Characteristics Module for Autistic Adults and the Creation of a Communication Profile Variable
papers.abstract: PurposeAutistic adults have diverse communication characteristics that are not well captured by standard demographic measures. Communication affects self-determination, relationships, access to healthcare, and services. Characterizing communication differences may improve research and intervention targeting for meaningful subgroups of autistic adults. MethodsThe Academic Autism Spectrum Partnership in Research and Education (AASPIRE) Outcomes Project team used a community based participatory research (CBPR) approach to develop a self- or caregiver-report module to characterize communication among autistic adults. The 10-item module asks about receptive and expressive communication, literacy, speech reliability, usage of digital communication, use of alternatives to speech, and communication fluency. It can be completed directly, with or without support, or via a caregiver. We used baseline survey data from 844 autistic adults to evaluate the module and derived a five-level variable, Communication Profile, from selected module items to stratify participants. We examined completion feasibility, response consistency, and construct validity. We also assessed test-retest reliability in a 15% random subsample who completed a 2-week retest following the 6-month survey, with oversampling of caregiver-report respondents. ResultsThe Communication Characteristics module demonstrated high completion feasibility, minimal systematic error, and strong construct validity. The Communication Profile variable stratified participants into five meaningful communication profiles and demonstrated strong construct validity and substantial test-retest reliability (weighted K = .69). ConclusionThe Communication Characteristics module and Communication Profile variable provide a valid approach for characterizing communication diversity among autistic adults for research, clinical, and service settings. The full AASPIRE Measurement Toolkit is available at https://aaspire.org/measurement. Lay SummaryAutistic people communicate in many different ways, and a persons communication may change in different situations. We developed and tested a set of survey questions to describe an individuals communication. We also used the results to describe 5 groups of autistic people based on how they communicate, without treating these groups as different types of autism.

papers.title: Preliminary Validation of a Multidimensional Stimulability Testing Rating Scale for Patients with Voice Disorders
papers.abstract: PurposeStimulability testing involves the evaluation of multiple aspects of a patients behavior, but the results are most frequently consolidated into a single domain (i.e., "stimulable"). The current study performs preliminary content, construct, concurrent, and predictive validation for the Multidimensional Stimulability Profile for Voice (MSP-V), a rating scale designed to measure multiple domains during stimulability testing (Degree of Change, Rapidity of Change, Generalization, Patient-rated Voice Quality, Patient-rated Voice Feel, and an overall rating of Stimulability Level). Methods78 patients with voice disorders (24 functional, 15 structural, 39 neurological) were administered the MSP-V by five speech-language pathologists (SLPs). Content validity was evaluated via the Content Validity Index (CVI) completed by nine voice-specialized SLPs. Construct validity was evaluated via exploratory factor analysis. Concurrent validity was assessed by determining whether MSP-V domains scaled in the expected direction compared to categorical stimulability ratings (e.g., "Highly stimulable" vs. Stimulable"). Predictive validity was assessed by examining the relationship between MSP-V domains and voice disorder diagnosis, return to voice therapy, and patient-reported practice outside of therapy. ResultsThe CVI reached the critical value for clinician-rated and patient-rated domains. Two distinct factors were identified during EFA, one consisting of clinician-rated domains and the other of patient-rated domains. All MSP-V domains showed the expected directional relationships as categorical stimulability ratings. No domains differed significantly between disorder etiologies. The Rapidity of Change and Stimulability Level domains both significantly predicted return for voice therapy, where participants who rated lower on each domain were more likely to return to for voice therapy. No domains were predictive of patient-reported practice. ConclusionsThe MSP-V is a clinically feasible tool with emerging content, construct, concurrent, and predictive validity that could be used to provide increased clarity and precision in stimulability testing documentation for research and practice.

papers.title: Feasibility and Measurement Properties of a Large Language Model-Based Virtual Patient Laboratory for Clinical Reasoning Training in Physical Therapy Students: Single-Arm Pilot Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) configured as virtual patients may expand structured practice of clinical reasoning in health professions education. Before testing effectiveness, it must be established whether students engage with them and whether the resulting scores are complete, reliable, and related to performance with real patients. Our earlier pilot randomized trial found very low engagement with a less structured LLM-based approach. ObjectiveThis study aimed to assess the feasibility (adherence, acceptability, and data completeness) of a revised, structured LLM-based clinical reasoning laboratory (Laboratorio de Inteligencia Artificial [LIA]) in undergraduate physical therapy education and to explore its measurement properties, including its association with clinical judgment with a real patient assessed with the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR). MethodsIn this single-arm pilot feasibility study, 27 third-year physical therapy students at a Spanish university completed, in 2024-2025, 3 virtual patient cases (lumbar, cervical, and thoracic spine pain) simulated by ChatGPT (GPT-4) over 4 weeks, each twice. ChatGPT scored each attempt from 0 to 4 on the same 10 dimensions of the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR; 0-40 points) that human assessors applied (1-4 per dimension; 10-40 points) during a real patient encounter. Feasibility outcomes were case completion, data completeness, and satisfaction (0-10). Measurement outcomes were internal consistency and convergent validity (Spearman correlations between model-generated and human LCJR scores). Variability estimates informed the sample size of a future trial. ResultsAll 27 students were assessed with the LCJR; 22 (81%) completed at least 1 LIA case. Both attempts of the lumbar, cervical, and thoracic cases were completed by 78%, 63%, and 74% of students, respectively. Satisfaction data were available for 15 students (56%; mean 6.0, SD 1.3), and missing secondary data clustered in the third rotation. Internal consistency was excellent for the LCJR (=.96) and ranged from .43 to .90 for model-generated ratings. Model-generated LIA scores clustered near the maximum (mean 36.0, SD 1.4). Among completers, LIA scores correlated weakly with the LCJR ({rho}=0.25, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.61; {rho}=0.44, 95% CI 0.05-0.71, when noncompleted attempts were scored as 0). Grade point average correlated almost perfectly with the LCJR ({rho}=0.96; n=22); after adjustment for it, the LIA-LCJR association disappeared (partial {rho}=-0.10). A future trial would require approximately 39 students per group (80% power, conservative variance). ConclusionsDelivering the LIA within the curriculum was feasible, but clinical judgment ratings generated by ChatGPT did not reflect those of human assessors with a real patient: they clustered near the maximum and showed no convergent validity once noncompletion was separated from performance. LLM-generated ratings should not be used as outcome or assessment measures without validation against human raters. Case calibration, completion tracking, and clarification of the GPA-LCJR relationship are also needed before a definitive trial. Trial RegistrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT06809634; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06809634

papers.title: Efficacy of physiotherapy in reducing pain in subjects with temporomandibular disorders: a systematic review with network meta-analysis
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTemporomandibular disorders are common conditions in the general population. Several therapeutic approaches are available, but there is no consensus on the most effective, particularly in physiotherapy. The objective of this review is to assess the effect of manual therapy and therapeutic exercise in reducing pain in patients with temporomandibular disorders. Data sourcesFour databases (MEDLINE, PEDro, EMBASE, CINAHL) were searched up to March 2025. Review methodsWe included randomized controlled trials evaluating the effects of manual therapy and/or therapeutic exercise in individuals with temporomandibular disorders, compared to any other rehabilitation treatment, with pain intensity as the primary outcome. The methodological quality was assessed using the PEDro scale. A network meta-analysis was performed to compare the effect of different rehabilitative approaches. Results25 randomised clinical trials for a total of 1,540 people were included. The main comparisons were: manual therapy and/or therapeutic exercise vs no treatment or placebo, occlusal splint, and instrumental physiotherapy. In most studies, manual therapy and therapeutic exercise were more effective than controls in reducing pain. However, the network meta-analysis indicated that multimodal treatments were the most effective. The methodological quality of the included studies ranged from 3 to 9 points. Conclusionmanual therapy and therapeutic exercise are effective strategies for reducing pain in subjects with temporomandibular disorders and should be used as first-line interventions before more invasive treatments; the combination of dry needling and manual therapy appears to be the most effective approach. Nonetheless, the variability in study quality suggests that further high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Extracting meaningful features from time series analysis of plasma analytes in clinical research
papers.abstract: While absolute blood biomarkers have long guided diagnosis, their rate of change often provides greater diagnostic value. For the Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophies studied here, increased muscle weakness is associated with abnormal sarcolemma repair. Time course analyses were made to changes in muscle-derived plasma enzymes after modest physical activity of ambulatory inpatients. Blood samples at 20 selected time points at variable intervals were obtained at rest, and before and after routine morning activities and motor function testing. After these activities, plasma enzyme levels increased in a similar way, suggesting damage and leakage from skeletal muscle. The levels then decreased in a similar way, suggesting that muscle cells stopped leaking and enzymes were subsequently cleared from the blood. The complex temporal changes were modeled using both continuous time and data features to reduce the number of parameters required to describe the irregularly sampled, interrupted, time series data. Unlike individuals with cardiac muscle ischemia or following intense exercise, there was no extended post-injury rising phase of enzyme levels. In contradistinction, levels fell once activity ceased. Time series analyses of blood biomarkers most likely provide an assay and index of sarcolemma fragility and by extension skeletal muscle damage.

papers.title: A normative torque-profile approach for quantifying elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance after stroke: a proof-of-principle study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPost-stroke spasticity is commonly assessed using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS), despite its limited objectivity and variable reliability. This study introduces ScoreE, a novel isokinetic dynamometry-derived metric designed to quantify elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance by comparing patients torque-angle profiles with a healthy reference corridor. MethodsThirty-five post-stroke patients and twenty-one healthy controls were included. Elbow and wrist hyper-resistance was assessed using the MAS and an isokinetic dynamometer in two testing conditions: seated on the dynamometer chair (ergo chair) and seated in the patients wheelchair. Two dynamometer-derived metrics were analyzed: ScoreE and peak torque (Peak{tau}). Feasibility, inter-rater and test-retest reliability, and associations with MAS grades were assessed. Exploratory PRE-POST changes following a 10-min local vibration session were also described. ResultsScoreE showed good to excellent inter-rater and test-retest reliability across joints and testing conditions. Inter-rater ICCs ranged from 0.81 to 0.89, and test-retest ICCs from 0.76 to 0.93. Peak{tau} showed moderate to good reliability. In contrast, MAS agreement was lower and more variable. ScoreE showed moderate associations with MAS grades, particularly at the elbow, with weaker and less consistent associations at the wrist. MAS assessment was faster, but all assessments were well tolerated, with median pain ratings of 0/10 in all testing conditions. PRE-POST vibration changes were small and heterogeneous, preventing formal assessment of responsiveness. ConclusionScoreE provides a reliable, objective, and visually interpretable quantification of post-stroke elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance. By comparing the full torque-angle profile with normative data, this approach preserves information on both the magnitude and angular span of abnormal resistance, supporting its potential for targeted longitudinal monitoring.
